a: or he may grow hard and refuse to obey you
t: A closing line: 'grief to you from him'
p: The Hebrew of MS B and the Latin end the verse with grief for the father. It goes with the variant at the start of the verse.

a: so that he does not stumble and disgrace you
p: Vaticanus speaks of 'your' disgrace; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi of 'his' shameful conduct, which trips you up.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἵνα μὴ ἐν τῇ ἀσχημοσύνῃ σου προσκόψῃ
readings.en: so that he does not stumble, to your shame
readings.plain: so that he does not stumble and disgrace you

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A) and Ephraemi (C), as Swete's notes give them; the KJV ("lest his lewd behaviour be an offence unto thee") and the Latin agree in sense
readings.orig: ἵνα μὴ ἐν τῇ ἀσχημοσύνῃ αὐτοῦ προσκόψῃς
readings.en: so that you do not stumble over his shameful conduct
readings.plain: so that his shameful ways do not trip you up

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus, its base text; the meaning is close either way. The other codices read more smoothly, which may be why they changed the pronouns.
b: Codex Ephraemi also has "while he is a child" in place of "and work hard at him," a line taken from the verse before.

a: or than a sickness that never leaves
p: A corrector of Sinaiticus, the Hebrew of MS B and the Latin read 'and eternal rest' is better than lasting sickness.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete; first hand of Sinaiticus; Alexandrinus; Ephraemi; the KJV
readings.orig: κρείσσων θάνατος ὑπὲρ ζωὴν πικρὰν ἢ ἀρρώστημα ἔμμονον
readings.en: Death is better than a bitter life or a lasting illness
readings.plain: or than a sickness that never leaves

readings.w: A corrector of Sinaiticus (ℵc.a), adding καὶ ἀνάπαυσις αἰώνιος; Hebrew of MS B, folio III recto, line 9 (ונוחת עולם); Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 30:17 (requies aeterna)
readings.orig: καὶ ἀνάπαυσις αἰώνιος ... ἢ ἀρρώστημα ἔμμονον
readings.en: and eternal rest (is better) than a lasting illness
readings.plain: and eternal rest than a sickness that never leaves

why: The Plain follows its base text. The Hebrew of MS B has 'everlasting rest' too, so the corrector of Sinaiticus brought the Greek in line with a reading the Hebrew also has. 'Eternal rest' here means the sleep of death, not a heavenly reward.

a: So it is with the one whom the Lord is hounding.
t: The sick man, or the rich man?
p: The Greek compares the sick man to an idol at a feast; the Hebrew of MS B compares a rich man who cannot enjoy his wealth.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices
readings.en: So is the one pursued by the Lord
readings.plain: So it is with the one whom the Lord is hounding.

readings.en: So is one who has wealth and does not enjoy it
readings.plain: So it is with one who has wealth / and gets no pleasure from it.

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 30:20; Douay-Rheims
readings.orig: Sic qui effugatur a Domino, portans mercedes iniquitatis
readings.en: So is he that is driven away by the Lord, bearing the reward of iniquity
readings.plain: So it is with the one whom the Lord drives away, / carrying the wages of his wrongdoing.

why: The Plain follows the Greek, its base text. The Hebrew line fits the setting of food (30:18); the Greek points toward sickness as God's punishment.

a: like a eunuch who holds a young woman in his arms and groans
t: An added line: 'so is one who does justice by force'
p: A later hand in Vaticanus and the Hebrew of MS B add the line found at 20:4.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete (the first hand), with Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus
readings.orig: ὥσπερ εὐνοῦχος περιλαμβάνων παρθένον καὶ στενάζων
readings.en: as a eunuch embracing a virgin and groaning
readings.plain: like a eunuch who holds a young woman in his arms and groans

readings.w: A corrector of Vaticanus (Bᵇ) in the margin; Hebrew of MS B, folio III recto, line 12

readings.plain: like a eunuch who holds a young woman in his arms and groans. / So is the one who does justice by force

why: The Plain follows the first hand. The added line is the end of 20:4 and may have come in from there, though MS B has it here too.

a: treat him like yourself
p: Vaticanus repeats 'like yourself'; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, the Hebrew of MS E, the Latin and the KJV say 'like a brother'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete
readings.en: treat him as yourself
readings.plain: treat him like yourself

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi, as Swete's notes give them; Hebrew of MS E, folio I verso, line 19 (אחד עבדך כאח, "Have you one slave? Like a brother..."); Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 33:31 (quasi fratrem); the KJV (33:31, "entreat him as a brother")
readings.en: treat him as a brother
readings.plain: treat him like a brother

why: The Plain follows its base text. 'Brother' has the Hebrew of MS E on its side, and Vaticanus's 'yourself' repeats the first line; but both readings say the same thing.

a: A well-taught man knows many things
p: Vaticanus reads 'a well-taught man'; Sinaiticus and the first hand of Alexandrinus read 'a man who has traveled'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete; a corrector of Alexandrinus
readings.en: An educated man knew many things
readings.plain: A well-taught man knows many things

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and the first hand of Alexandrinus (Swete reads A's first hand with a query: A*vid); the KJV (34:9, "A man that hath travelled")
readings.en: A man who has wandered knew many things
readings.plain: A man who has traveled knows many things

why: The Plain follows its base text. 'Traveled' fits 31:10–12, where the same verb ("wandered") follows, and may be original; 'taught' fits the book's praise of learning. The two words differ by a few letters in Greek.

a: an offering made in mockery
p: Alexandrinus reads 'blemished' for 'mocked', and so does the Latin. The variant in 31:22 goes with this one.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with Sinaiticus
readings.en: a mocked offering
readings.plain: an offering made in mockery

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes); Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 34:21 (maculata)
readings.en: a blemished offering
readings.plain: an offering with a blemish

why: The Plain follows its base text. 'Blemished' fits the language of sacrifice (offerings had to be without blemish, Leviticus 22:20); the two Greek words differ by one letter.

a: the mockeries of lawless men
p: A corrector of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read 'blemishes'; a note in Sinaiticus's margin reads 'gifts'. Goes with 31:21.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete
readings.en: mockeries of the lawless
readings.plain: the mockeries of lawless men

readings.w: A corrector of Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes)
readings.en: blemishes of the lawless
readings.plain: the blemished gifts of lawless men

readings.w: A marginal note in Sinaiticus (Swete's notes); the KJV (34:18, "the gifts of unjust men")
readings.en: gifts of the lawless
readings.plain: the gifts of lawless men

why: The Plain follows its base text, keeping the wordplay with 31:21.

a: Whoever keeps the law piles up contributions;
p: Swete prints symphoras, 'things brought together'; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read prosphoras, 'offerings', as the Latin and the KJV do.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete
readings.en: The one who keeps the law multiplies contributions
readings.plain: Whoever keeps the law piles up contributions;

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (Swete's notes); Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 35:1 (multiplicat oblationem); the KJV (35:1, "bringeth offerings enough")
readings.en: The one who keeps the law multiplies offerings
readings.plain: Whoever keeps the law brings offerings in plenty;

why: The Plain follows Swete's word. Liddell, Scott and Jones give symphora first as 'a bringing together' and, in a later writer, 'a contribution', though its common sense is 'event' or 'misfortune'; 'contributions' is the sense that fits a list of offerings (32:2–4). The 'offerings' of Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and the Latin say it more plainly. No Hebrew manuscript read for this site covers the verse: MS B has a gap here, and its next leaf begins at 32:11.

a: Have mercy on us, Master, God of all
p: Alexandrinus leaves out 'Master'; the Hebrew of MS B begins 'Save us, God of all'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with Sinaiticus
readings.orig: Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς, δέσποτα ὁ θεὸς πάντων

readings.plain: Have mercy on us, Master, God of all

readings.plain: Have mercy on us, God of all

readings.en: Save us, God of all
readings.plain: Save us, God of all

why: The Plain follows its base text. The Hebrew 'save us' is the cry of Psalm 106:47; the Greek 'have mercy' is the opening of many prayers.

a: cast the fear of you on all the nations
t: 'The nations that have not sought you'
p: The Latin and the KJV add 'that have not sought you'. The Greek and the Hebrew of MS B do not.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices; Hebrew of MS B, folio VI verso, line 1 ("...your fear on all the nations," the verb damaged)
readings.orig: ἐπίβαλε τὸν φόβον σου ἐπὶ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη
readings.en: cast your fear on all the nations
readings.plain: cast the fear of you on all the nations

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:2; the KJV (36:2, "that seek not after thee")
readings.orig: immitte timorem tuum super gentes quæ non exquisierunt te
readings.en: send your fear on the nations that have not sought you
readings.plain: cast the fear of you on all the nations that have not sought you

why: The Plain follows the Greek; the Hebrew of MS B agrees with it in having no limit. The Latin narrows the prayer to the nations that do not seek God.

a: Hurry the time and remember your oath
p: The Hebrew of MS B asks God to hurry 'the end' and appoint 'the set time'; the Latin says 'remember the end'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices
readings.en: Hasten the time and remember the oath
readings.plain: Hurry the time and remember your oath

readings.w: Hebrew of MS B, folio VI verso, line 7
readings.orig: החיש קץ ופקוד מועד כי מי יאמר לך מה תעשה
readings.en: Hasten the end and appoint the set time, for who can say to you, 'What are you doing?'
readings.plain: Hurry the end and appoint the set time

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:10; the KJV (36:8, "remember the covenant")
readings.en: Hasten the time, and remember the end
readings.plain: Hurry the time and remember the end

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew's 'end' (qets) and 'set time' (mo'ed) are the words of Habakkuk 2:3 and Daniel 8:19; the Hebrew also adds a line that the Greek lacks.

a: Smash the heads of the enemy's rulers
p: Where the Greek has 'rulers of the enemies', the Hebrew of MS B names Moab, in the words of Balaam's oracle; its margin reads 'enemy'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices; Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:12; the KJV (36:10, "the rulers of the heathen")
readings.en: Crush the heads of the rulers of enemies
readings.plain: Smash the heads of the enemy's rulers

readings.w: Hebrew of MS B, folio VI verso, line 8 (the margin reads אויב, "enemy," for "Moab")
readings.en: Put an end to the head of the brows of Moab
readings.plain: Make an end of the brows of Moab

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew takes up Numbers 24:17, "It will smash the brows of Moab," with 'Moab' standing for Israel's enemies; its second line is singular, "who says, 'There is no one but me.'" The margin of MS B reads 'enemy' in place of 'Moab', the word the Greek has.
b: Moab had long ceased to be a power in Ben Sira's time, so the Hebrew uses it as a name for the enemy, as Isaiah 25:10 and Balaam's oracle do.

a: trips up those who sacrifice to it
t: 'Sacrifice to it' or 'are mad about it'?
p: Vaticanus reads 'sacrifice to it'; the first hand of Sinaiticus reads 'are possessed by it'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete; a corrector of Sinaiticus; the KJV (31:7, "them that sacrifice unto it")
readings.en: to those who sacrifice to it
readings.plain: trips up those who sacrifice to it

readings.w: The first hand of Sinaiticus (Swete's notes)
readings.en: to those who are wildly devoted to it
readings.plain: trips up those who are mad about it

why: The Plain follows its base text. The two Greek words differ by one letter; 'mad about it' gives English its 'enthusiasm', but 'sacrifice' fits the picture of gold as an idol.

a: get up halfway through the meal
p: Swete prints mesoporōn, the reading of a corrector of Sinaiticus; Vaticanus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi spell mesopōrōn; the Latin says 'vomit'.

readings.w: Swete's text, the reading of a corrector of Sinaiticus (ℵc.a)
readings.en: get up, being halfway
readings.plain: get up halfway through the meal

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi (Swete's notes: μεσοπωρων); the first hand of Sinaiticus has μεσοπωρον
readings.en: get up (a spelling of the same word with ω)
readings.plain: get up halfway through the meal

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 31:25; the KJV (31:21, "arise, go forth, vomit"); compare the second form of the line in the Hebrew of MS B, folio IV verso, line 2
readings.en: get up from the middle, vomit
readings.plain: get up and leave the table, and vomit

why: Swete prints the corrected reading of Sinaiticus against Vaticanus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi; their mesopōrōn is not a known Greek word and reads as a misspelling of mesoporōn, which Liddell, Scott and Jones give as 'be halfway', used of a meal at this verse. The Plain follows Swete. 'Vomit' is in the Latin and in one line of MS B, not in the Greek.

a: will accept discipline
p: Swete prints the first hand of Vaticanus, spelling paidian; the corrected Vaticanus and Alexandrinus spell paideian, 'discipline'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, first hand, as Swete prints it (his notes give the spelling παιδείαν for the correctors of B and for A, and nothing for Sinaiticus)
readings.en: will receive paidian, a spelling of paideian
readings.plain: will accept discipline

readings.w: Correctors of Vaticanus (Bᵃᵇ) and Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes); the KJV (32:14, "his discipline"); Hebrew of MS B, folio V verso, line 1 (יקח מוסר)
readings.en: will receive discipline
readings.plain: will accept discipline

readings.w: A corrector of Vaticanus (Bᵇ), in Swete's notes
readings.en: will choose
readings.plain: will choose discipline

why: The Plain here departs from the letters Swete prints. In the codices of this period the letters ει and ι were pronounced alike and often confused, so the first hand's paidian can be read as a spelling of paideian, 'discipline', the reading of B's correctors and of A. The Hebrew musar, 'discipline', in MS B confirms the sense.

a: and guard yourself against your own children
p: The Greek says 'guard yourself against your children'; the Hebrew says 'beware of your end'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices; Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 32:26; the KJV (32:22)
readings.orig: καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν τέκνων σου φύλαξαι
readings.en: and guard yourself from your children
readings.plain: and guard yourself against your own children

readings.w: Hebrew of MS B, folio V verso, line 11; MS E, folio I recto, line 8, and MS F, folio I verso, line 12, read ובאחריתך היה זהיר, 'and be careful about your end'
readings.en: and beware of your end
readings.plain: and beware of what comes after you

readings.w: Hebrew of MS B, folio V verso, line 12 (a second form of the saying)
readings.en: and be careful in your paths
readings.plain: and be careful on your paths

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew fits the road picture of 35:20–21 better; its acharit, 'end', can also mean descendants, which may lie behind the Greek 'children'. See the note on the word.

a: In everything you do, trust yourself
p: The Greek says 'trust your soul'; the Hebrew says 'guard your soul'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices; the KJV (32:23, "trust thy own soul")
readings.orig: ἐν παντὶ ἔργῳ πίστευε τῇ ψυχῇ σου
readings.en: in every work trust your soul
readings.plain: In everything you do, trust yourself

readings.w: Hebrew of MS B, folio V verso, line 14 (line 13 has "in all your ways")
readings.en: in all your deeds guard yourself
readings.plain: In everything you do, guard yourself

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew 'guard' fits the warnings of 35:20–22; in Greek the verbs for 'guard' and 'trust' are not alike, so the difference goes back to the Hebrew wording or to the translation.

a: as an inquiry made by the righteous
p: Vaticanus reads 'of the righteous'; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read the Septuagint's word for the Urim.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete
readings.en: as an inquiry of the righteous
readings.plain: as an inquiry made by the righteous

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (Swete's notes)
readings.en: as an inquiry of the Urim
readings.plain: as an inquiry made by the Urim

why: The Plain follows its base text. The reading of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus has much in its favor: their δήλων is the Septuagint's word for the Urim (Numbers 27:21), while δικαίων, 'of the righteous', is a commoner word a copyist could have put in its place.
b: The Hebrew of MS B breaks off after "and his law" (folio V verso, line 18), and MS E and MS F leave out the verse. Kahana's 1912 edition prints the line as ending "like the Urim in the breastpiece"; those words are not in Abegg's transcription of the leaf, so they are not given here as a reading of the manuscript.

a: and you will give them their inheritance as at the beginning
t: 'You will give them' or 'I gave them'?
p: Swete prints 'you will give them', with a pointer to his preface; Vaticanus, Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read 'I gave them their inheritance'.

readings.w: Swete's text, which his note marks "vid praef" (see the preface; the preface was not read for this site); Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:13 (et hæreditabis eos); the KJV (36:11, "and inherit thou them")
readings.orig: καὶ κατακληρονομήσεις αὐτοὺς καθὼς ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς
readings.en: and you will give them inheritance as from the beginning
readings.plain: and you will give them their inheritance as at the beginning

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (Swete's notes)
readings.orig: καὶ κατεκληρονόμησα αὐτοὺς καθὼς ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς
readings.en: and I gave them inheritance as from the beginning
readings.plain: and I gave them their inheritance as at the beginning

readings.w: Hebrew of MS B, folio VI verso, line 9
readings.en: and let them take their inheritance as in days of old
readings.plain: and let them take their inheritance as in days of old

why: The best Greek witnesses, Vaticanus, Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, all read 'I gave them'; the printed 'you will give them' is Swete's text against them. The Plain follows Swete, and the Hebrew of MS B and the Latin agree with his sense. A guess, not a shown fact: the 'I' may have come from the first half of the verse, 'I too kept watch', which the swapped blocks set beside this half-line.

a: with the praise of your mighty deeds
t: 'Praise of your deeds', 'lift up your oracles' or 'your majesty'?
p: Vaticanus reads one rare word; correctors and other codices split it into 'to lift up your oracles'; the Hebrew of MS B says 'your majesty'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete (first hand)
readings.en: fill Zion with the telling of your mighty deeds
readings.plain: with the praise of your mighty deeds

readings.w: A corrector of Vaticanus, Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (Swete's notes)
readings.orig: πλῆσον Σιὼν ἆραι τὰ λόγιά σου
readings.en: fill Zion, to lift up your oracles
readings.plain: so it may lift up your oracles

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:16; the KJV (36:14, "thine unspeakable oracles")
readings.en: Fill Zion with your words beyond telling
readings.plain: with your words beyond telling

readings.w: Hebrew of MS B, folio VI verso, line 12 (margin: מהדריך, "your splendors")
readings.en: Fill Zion with your majesty
readings.plain: with your majesty

why: The Plain follows its base text. Aretalogia, the recital of a god's mighty deeds, was a rare word; later copyists divided its letters into commoner words, which gave the KJV's 'oracles'.

a: fill your people with your glory
p: The Greek has 'your people'; the Hebrew of MS B has 'your temple'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices; Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:16; the KJV
readings.orig: καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς δόξης σου τὸν λαόν σου
readings.en: and your people from your glory
readings.plain: fill your people with your glory

readings.w: Hebrew of MS B, folio VI verso, line 12
readings.en: and your temple with your glory
readings.plain: fill your temple with your glory

why: The Plain follows the Greek. In Greek 'people' (laon) and 'temple' (naon) differ by one letter, so a copyist's slip early in the Greek may explain it; the Hebrew, with Zion in the first line, speaks of the temple, as in Haggai 2:7.

a: the prayer of those who plead with you
p: Vaticanus reads 'suppliants'; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read 'servants', as do the Latin, the Hebrew of MS B and the KJV.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete
readings.en: the prayer of your suppliants
readings.plain: the prayer of those who plead with you

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (Swete's notes); Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:18 (servorum tuorum); Hebrew of MS B, folio VI verso, line 15 (עבדיך); the KJV (36:17)
readings.en: the prayer of your servants
readings.plain: the prayer of your servants

why: The Plain follows its base text. The two Greek words differ by one letter, and the Hebrew 'your servants' supports the reading of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus.

a: as Aaron blessed your people.
p: The Greek and the Latin speak of the blessing of Aaron; the Hebrew of MS B says 'according to your goodwill toward your people'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices; Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:19; the KJV (36:17)
readings.orig: κατὰ τὴν εὐλογίαν Ἀαρὼν περὶ τοῦ λαοῦ σου
readings.en: according to the blessing of Aaron for your people
readings.plain: as Aaron blessed your people.

readings.w: Hebrew of MS B, folio VI verso, line 15 (margin: ברצונך, "in your goodwill")
readings.en: according to your goodwill toward your people
readings.plain: in your goodwill toward your people.

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew of MS B is simpler; the Greek may come from a Hebrew copy that read birkat, 'blessing', in place of the word for goodwill.

a: who strays from town to town?
p: Swete prints sphallomenō, 'going astray'; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read aphallomenō, 'leaping off'; the Hebrew has 'skipping'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete
readings.orig: εὐζώνῳ λῃστῇ σφαλλομένῳ ἐκ πόλεως εἰς πόλιν
readings.en: a well-girded robber going astray from city to city
readings.plain: who strays from town to town?

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (Swete's notes: αφαλλομενω)
readings.orig: εὐζώνῳ λῃστῇ ἀφαλλομένῳ ἐκ πόλεως εἰς πόλιν
readings.en: a well-girded robber springing off from city to city
readings.plain: who leaps from town to town?

readings.w: Hebrew of MS B, folio VII recto, line 8; also MS D, folio II recto, lines 2–3, and MS C, folio VIII verso, lines 7–9 (damaged)
readings.orig: מי יאמין בגדוד צבא המדלג מעיר אל עיר
readings.en: who will trust a band of soldiers that skips from city to city?
readings.plain: that skips from town to town?

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:28; the KJV (36:26, "a thief well appointed, that skippeth from city to city")
readings.orig: quasi succinctus latro exiliens de civitate in civitatem
readings.en: like a robber girded up, leaping out from city to city
readings.plain: who leaps from town to town?

why: The Plain follows its base text. Liddell, Scott and Jones give sphallomai as 'be tripped up, fall' and 'err, go astray', and aphallomai as 'spring off'. The reading of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agrees with the Hebrew's 'skips' and the Latin's 'leaping', and the two Greek words differ by a letter or two.
